newsitem.title: CHINA: Gore assures China in funds flap, sees rosy future.
newsitem.headline: Gore assures China in funds flap, sees rosy future.

text.p: U.S. Vice President Al Gore on Wednesday offered his Chinese hosts rosy messages on future ties after assuring Beijing that Washington's policies would not immediately change over a simmering political funding scandal.

"Our vision is that the U.S. and China, as friends and partners, will share a prosperous and peaceful future of free minds and free markets," Gore told a gathering of students at the prestigious Qinghua University.

However, Gore warned in talks with Premier Li Peng on Tuesday that Wasington would regard the matter very seriously if charges Beijing tried to illegally fund U.S. Democratic Party politicians were proved true, a senior U.S. official said.
"It is premature to say that an investigation that hasn't been completed yet is going to have a major impact on the relationship," said the official who declined to be identified.
"If the allegations are later proven to be true then they are very serious and we'll deal with it at that time," said the official, who took part in the talks between Gore and Li.

Gore met President and Communist Party chief Jiang Zemin on Wednesday, and both leaders painted an upbeat picture of the visit by Gore, the highest-ranking U.S. official to come to China since the 1989 crackdown on student demonstrations.
"The past two days have been very productive," Jiang told Gore as the two sat down for talks. "I believe we can actually have a chat in a light atmosphere today."

In his speech at Qinghua, Gore alluded to the issue of human rights -- one of many thorns that have marred Sino-U.S. ties -- by hinting that Beijing's economic liberalisation could ultimately lead to more political freedoms.
"We believe economic freedom and political freedom are part of an interlinked system and ultimately rely on one another," Gore said.

"China is in the process of a profound change and on its way to becoming something very different from what it has been," he told the university, which was a centre of the 1989 student-led demonstrations that the army crushed with heavy loss of life.

China's Li raised the political payments flap in Tuesday's meeting with Gore and vigorously denied that Beijing had sent funds into campaign coffers of Democratic Party candidates in the 1996 elections, the official said.
But one U.S. official quoted Gore as telling Li: "The controversy is of no consequence if the allegations turn out to be untrue. If they are true, then that is another matter."

The official was seeking to qualify comments by a colleague who on Tuesday stressed that Gore used the talks to assure China there would be no change in the U.S. policy of engagement because of the controversy.
China's Li had responded by saying he was reassured this would not affect Washington's pledges to improve ties with Beijing, the official said on Tuesday.

The Washington Post has reported that the Federal Bureau of Investigation warned six members of Congress last year they had been targeted by China to receive illegal campaign funds from foreign corporations.
The fundraising uproar is particularly sensitive for Gore, because he and U.S. President Bill Clinton have been accused of questionable fund raising practices in their re-election campaign.

The Democratic Party was forced to say it was refunding some $3 million in contributions after an investigation suggested the money may have come from illegal sources, many from various interests in Asia.
